Lecture 31

The wave equation and d’Alembert’s formula

Lecture objectives

We find the characteristic lines of the wave equation, write every solution as a sum of two travelling waves and derive d’Alembert’s formula for the infinite string. We prove the conservation of energy and the uniqueness it gives on a bounded string, and give a plucked string a precisely stated weaker solution.

Lecture 29 derived the equation utt=c2uxx+f/ρu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}+f/\rhoutt​=c2uxx​+f/ρ of a stretched string with the wave speed c=T/ρ.c=\sqrt{T/\rho}c=T/ρ​. In this lecture we solve it without external force on the whole line. This infinite string models a long string far from its ends, before a disturbance reaches an end. The lecture reads in three stages: characteristics and d’Alembert’s formula (Sections 31.1–31.3), pulses and energy (Sections 31.4–31.5), and the plucked string and the fixed end (Sections 31.6–31.7).

31.1 Characteristics of the wave operator

Throughout the lecture c>0c>0c>0 is a constant, and the wave equation is utt=c2uxx.u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}.utt​=c2uxx​.(31.1) It is Lecture 29’s string equation with f=0,f=0f=0, and it is hyperbolic in Lecture 29’s classification. A classical solution on an open set is a function with continuous partial derivatives up to order two there that satisfies (31.1) at every point.

Lecture 29’s Cauchy data on a curve, the values of uuu and of its derivative across the curve, give uxu_xux​ and utu_tut​ on the curve. As Lecture 30 announced, the characteristic curves are those on which these values and the equation fail to determine the second derivatives.

Proposition 31.1 (Second derivatives from data on a curve). Let uuu be a classical solution of (31.1) on an open set that contains the curve μ↦(x(μ),t(μ))\mu\mapsto(x(\mu),t(\mu))μ↦(x(μ),t(μ)) on an open interval, with xxx and ttt continuously differentiable and (x′,t′)≠(0,0).(x',t')\ne(0,0)(x′,t′)=(0,0). Then at each point of the curve x′uxx+t′uxt= ⁣d ⁣dμ[ux(x(μ),t(μ))],x′uxt+t′utt= ⁣d ⁣dμ[ut(x(μ),t(μ))],−c2uxx+utt=0.\begin{aligned} x'u_{xx}+t'u_{xt}&=\frac{\dd}{\dd\mu}\bigl[u_x(x(\mu),t(\mu))\bigr],\\ x'u_{xt}+t'u_{tt}&=\frac{\dd}{\dd\mu}\bigl[u_t(x(\mu),t(\mu))\bigr],\\ -c^2u_{xx}+u_{tt}&=0 . \end{aligned}x′uxx​+t′uxt​x′uxt​+t′utt​−c2uxx​+utt​​=dμd​[ux​(x(μ),t(μ))],=dμd​[ut​(x(μ),t(μ))],=0.​(31.2) The determinant of this linear system for (uxx,uxt,utt)(u_{xx},u_{xt},u_{tt})(uxx​,uxt​,utt​) is x′2−c2t′2.x'^2-c^2t'^2x′2−c2t′2. At a point where x′2≠c2t′2,x'^2\ne c^2t'^2x′2=c2t′2, the values of uxu_xux​ and utu_tut​ along the curve determine the second derivatives.

Proof. The first two equations are the chain rule (GM 36) applied to uxu_xux​ and ut,u_tut​, which are continuously differentiable, along the curve. We use utx=uxtu_{tx}=u_{xt}utx​=uxt​ (Schwarz’s theorem, GM 37). The third is the wave equation. Expanding along the first row, det⁡(x′t′00x′t′−c201)=x′(x′−0)−t′(0+c2t′)=x′2−c2t′2.\det\begin{pmatrix}x'&t'&0\\0&x'&t'\\-c^2&0&1\end{pmatrix} =x'(x'-0)-t'\bigl(0+c^2t'\bigr)=x'^2-c^2t'^2 .det​x′0−c2​t′x′0​0t′1​​=x′(x′−0)−t′(0+c2t′)=x′2−c2t′2. Where it is nonzero, the system has exactly one solution. ■

Definition 31.2 (Characteristic curve of the wave operator). A characteristic curve of the wave operator ∂t2−c2∂x2\partial_t^2-c^2\partial_x^2∂t2​−c2∂x2​ is a curve μ↦(x(μ),t(μ))\mu\mapsto(x(\mu),t(\mu))μ↦(x(μ),t(μ)) on an open interval, with xxx and ttt continuously differentiable and (x′,t′)≠(0,0),(x',t')\ne(0,0)(x′,t′)=(0,0), such that x′(μ)2=c2 t′(μ)2for every μ.x'(\mu)^2=c^2\,t'(\mu)^2\qquad\text{for every }\mu .x′(μ)2=c2t′(μ)2for every μ.(31.3)

The characteristic curves lie on straight lines. Indeed, t′(μ)=0t'(\mu)=0t′(μ)=0 would give x′(μ)=0x'(\mu)=0x′(μ)=0 by (31.3), which is excluded. So the continuous t′t't′ has one sign, ttt is strictly monotone with a differentiable inverse μ(t)\mu(t)μ(t) (GM 8), and the curve is the graph of X(t)=x(μ(t))X(t)=x(\mu(t))X(t)=x(μ(t)) with X′=x′/t′.X'=x'/t'X′=x′/t′. By (31.3) the continuous function X′X'X′ takes only the values ccc and −c,-c−c, so by the intermediate value theorem (GM 6) it is constant. Therefore every characteristic curve lies on a line x−ct=constorx+ct=const.x-ct=\text{const}\qquad\text{or}\qquad x+ct=\text{const}.x−ct=constorx+ct=const.(31.4) These are the two families announced by Lecture 30. A disturbance that follows the first family moves to the right with the speed c,cc, and one that follows the second moves to the left.

Theorem 31.3 (General solution of the wave equation). Let uuu have continuous partial derivatives up to order two on the half-plane t>0.t>0t>0. Then uuu solves (31.1) there if and only if there are functions FFF and GGG with continuous second derivatives on R\RR such that u(x,t)=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)(x∈R, t>0).u(x,t)=F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)\qquad(x\in\R,\ t>0).u(x,t)=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)(x∈R, t>0).(31.7) The pair (F,G)(F,G)(F,G) is unique up to replacing it by (F+b,G−b)(F+b,G-b)(F+b,G−b) with a constant b.bb.

31.3 The Cauchy problem and d’Alembert’s formula

At t=0t=0t=0 the string has an initial displacement u0u_0u0​ and an initial velocity v0.v_0v0​. The wave equation is of second order in time, so it takes both, as Lecture 29 explained for Cauchy data. The line t=0t=0t=0 has the tangent (x′,t′)=(1,0),(x',t')=(1,0)(x′,t′)=(1,0), and 1≠0=c2t′2,1\ne0=c^2t'^21=0=c2t′2, so by Proposition 31.1 it is not characteristic.

Definition 31.4 (Classical solution of the Cauchy problem). Let u0u_0u0​ have a continuous second derivative and v0v_0v0​ a continuous first derivative on R.\RR. A classical solution of the Cauchy problem utt=c2uxx(x∈R, t>0),u(x,0)=u0(x),ut(x,0)=v0(x)(x∈R),u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\quad(x\in\R,\ t>0),\qquad u(x,0)=u_0(x),\qquad u_t(x,0)=v_0(x)\quad(x\in\R),utt​=c2uxx​(x∈R, t>0),u(x,0)=u0​(x),ut​(x,0)=v0​(x)(x∈R),(31.8) is a function uuu that is continuous on R×[0,∞),\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), has continuous partial derivatives up to order two on R×(0,∞),\R\times(0,\infty)R×(0,∞), with utu_tut​ extending continuously to R×[0,∞),\R\times[0,\infty)R×[0,∞), that solves the wave equation for t>0t>0t>0 and satisfies the two initial conditions. Here ut(x,0)u_t(x,0)ut​(x,0) is the value of the continuous extension.

Theorem 31.5 (d’Alembert’s formula). Under the hypotheses of Definition 31.4 the Cauchy problem (31.8) has exactly one classical solution. It is u(x,t)=12[u0(x−ct)+u0(x+ct)]+12c∫x−ctx+ctv0(y) ⁣dy.u(x,t)=\frac12\bigl[u_0(x-ct)+u_0(x+ct)\bigr]+\frac1{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}v_0(y)\dd y .u(x,t)=21​[u0​(x−ct)+u0​(x+ct)]+2c1​∫x−ctx+ct​v0​(y)dy.(31.9)

The formula has two parts. The displacement data split into two halves, one moving to the right and one to the left, each with half the original height. The velocity data enter through their integral over an interval that grows with time.

The value of uuu at a point (x0,t0)(x_0,t_0)(x0​,t0​) with t0>0t_0>0t0​>0 uses u0u_0u0​ only at the two points x0±ct0x_0\pm ct_0x0​±ct0​ and v0v_0v0​ only on the interval [x0−ct0,x0+ct0].[x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0][x0​−ct0​,x0​+ct0​]. This interval is the domain of dependence of the point. It is cut out of the initial line by the two characteristic lines through (x0,t0),(x_0,t_0)(x0​,t0​), which bound a triangle in the (x,t)(x,t)(x,t)-plane (Figure 31.1). Conversely, the data near a point x1x_1x1​ affect u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t) only if x1x_1x1​ lies in [x−ct,x+ct],[x-ct,x+ct][x−ct,x+ct], that is, only in the wedge ∣x−x1∣≤ct\abs{x-x_1}\le ct∣x−x1​∣≤ct above x1.x_1x1​. This wedge is the domain of influence of x1.x_1x1​. In particular, if u0u_0u0​ and v0v_0v0​ vanish outside an interval [x1,x2],[x_1,x_2][x1​,x2​], then u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1−ctorx>x2+ct.u(x,t)=0\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad x<x_1-ct\quad\text{or}\quad x>x_2+ct .u(x,t)=0wheneverx<x1​−ctorx>x2​+ct.(31.10) Disturbances travel with at most the speed c.cc. This property is called finite propagation speed.

Formula (31.9) also shows that the solution changes little when the data change little. This is the continuous dependence required of a well-posed problem in Lecture 29.

31.4 Displacement and velocity pulses

We now follow two pulses of the same shape, one given as a displacement and one as a velocity. We need a localized profile with two continuous derivatives whose integrals can be computed exactly. The bump profile B(y)={(1−y2)3,∣y∣<1,0,∣y∣≥1,B(y)=\begin{cases}(1-y^2)^3,&\abs y<1,\\ 0,&\abs y\ge1,\end{cases}B(y)={(1−y2)3,0,​∣y∣<1,∣y∣≥1,​(31.12) has this property. Example 31.7 (Displacement and velocity pulses). We compute the motion of a string from a displacement pulse and from a velocity pulse of the same shape, and we find which data determine the displacement at a given point. Let ℓ>0\ell>0ℓ>0 be the half-width of the pulse. 31.6 A plucked string and its weaker solution

A guitar string is plucked by pulling it aside at one point and releasing it. Its initial shape has a corner, so it does not have a second derivative there, and Theorem 31.5 does not apply. The formula of d’Alembert still makes sense, and we now state in which sense it solves the problem.

Summary

The wave operator has the characteristic lines x±ct=const.x\pm ct=\text{const}x±ct=const. In the coordinates α=x−ct\alpha=x-ctα=x−ct and β=x+ct\beta=x+ctβ=x+ct the wave equation becomes Wαβ=0,W_{\alpha\beta}=0Wαβ​=0, so every classical solution is a sum of a right-moving and a left-moving wave. The initial displacement and velocity fix these waves and give d’Alembert’s formula, which depends continuously on the data and propagates disturbances with at most the speed c.cc. The energy changes only by the power delivered at the ends, which proves uniqueness on a bounded string. A plucked string is described by the d’Alembert solution, a solution in the sense of distributions and a uniform limit of classical solutions.

  • Domains: u(x0,t0)u(x_0,t_0)u(x0​,t0​) depends on the data in [x0−ct0,x0+ct0];[x_0-ct_0,x_0+ct_0][x0​−ct0​,x0​+ct0​]; the data at x1x_1x1​ influence only ∣x−x1∣≤ct.\abs{x-x_1}\le ct∣x−x1​∣≤ct.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. For the wave equation utt=c2uxxu_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}utt​=c2uxx​ on the line with c>0c>0c>0, which statement describes the two profiles in u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x-ct)+G(x+ct)u=F(x−ct)+G(x+ct)?

Hint. Hold the argument of each profile constant as time increases.

For FFF, a fixed argument gives x=ct+Cx=ct+Cx=ct+C, so the profile moves right. For GGG, a fixed argument gives x=−ct+Cx=-ct+Cx=−ct+C, so it moves left. Reversing the signs reverses the two directions. Saying both move the same way ignores the opposite slopes. Initial velocity depends on the derivatives of both profiles, through ut(x,0)=−cF′(x)+cG′(x)u_t(x,0)=-cF'(x)+cG'(x)ut​(x,0)=−cF′(x)+cG′(x), so the profiles are not themselves the two initial data.

2. On an infinite string, use dimensionless variables with wave speed c=2c=2c=2, initial displacement u0(x)=x2u_0(x)=x^2u0​(x)=x2 and initial velocity v0(x)=2xv_0(x)=2xv0​(x)=2x. Find u(1,1)u(1,1)u(1,1) and round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Which initial data does d’Alembert’s formula sample only at the ends of the initial interval, and which does it integrate?

The initial interval is [1−2,1+2]=[−1,3][1-2,1+2]=[-1,3][1−2,1+2]=[−1,3]. The displacement contributes (1+9)/2=5(1+9)/2=5(1+9)/2=5 from its endpoints. The velocity contributes 14∫−132y ⁣dy=14(9−1)=2\frac14\int_{-1}^3 2y\dd y=\frac14(9-1)=241​∫−13​2ydy=41​(9−1)=2. Adding gives 777. Using only the endpoints for the velocity would omit its contribution throughout the interval.

3. For a small-slope string with linear density ρ=2 kg m−1\rho=2\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}ρ=2kgm−1 and tension T=8 NT=8\,\mathrm NT=8N, at a point the transverse velocity is ut=3 m s−1u_t=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}ut​=3ms−1 and the slope is ux=1/4u_x=1/4ux​=1/4. What is the energy per unit length there, in J m−1\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}Jm−1?

Hint. Add the kinetic and potential energy densities. Each is quadratic in its derivative.

The kinetic density is 12ρut2=9 J m−1\tfrac12\rho u_t^2=9\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}21​ρut2​=9Jm−1 and the potential density is 12Tux2=0.25 J m−1\tfrac12 Tu_x^2=0.25\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}21​Tux2​=0.25Jm−1. Their sum is 9.25 J m−19.25\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-1}}9.25Jm−1. The value 999 ignores the slope. The value 101010 uses the slope to the first power. The value 18.518.518.5 drops both factors of one half.

4. An infinite string starts with a continuous triangular displacement and zero velocity. In what sense does the resulting d’Alembert solution satisfy the wave equation when the corners propagate?

Hint. Think about what happens to a corner when the profile is translated, and how the derivatives can be transferred to a test function.

The two translated halves of the displacement are continuous and retain corners. Along a corner line the derivatives required of a classical solution can fail to exist. In the distributional identity, the wave operator acts on the test function. In characteristic coordinates it is proportional to a mixed derivative. Each travelling profile depends on just one of those coordinates, so integrating in the other one gives zero by compact support. This proves the equation across the corner lines and at positive times.
